claims.text: The initial material is cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Plasma electrolytic oxidation can produce a 1–2 μm Al2O3 coating on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
A 1–2 μm Al2O3 coating will improve the alloy's high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The coating will improve oxygen resistance without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
The proposed operating boundary is exposure at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours under a 500 MPa mechanical-loading boundary.
The Al2O3 coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion reduces the formation of embrittling oxides in HfNbTaTiZr.
Reducing embrittling-oxide formation preserves the alloy's ductility.
Relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, coating and exposure will increase room-temperature tensile ductility by 20–30%.
Relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, coating will decrease yield strength at 1000 °C by 10–20%.
Performance may vary with coating quality, thickness, uniformity, and testing conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says useful mechanical performance will not be sacrificed, but the predicted outcome explicitly allows a 10–20% decrease in high-temperature yield strength.

The prediction specifies a 20–30% ductility increase and a 10–20% yield-strength decrease, whereas the falsification rule accepts ductility increases as low as 10% and strength decreases as large as 30%; thus outcomes outside the predicted ranges could still pass.

The experimental design specifies only room-temperature tensile testing after exposure, but the measurements and falsification rule require yield strength at 1000 °C, for which no high-temperature mechanical test is specified.
